interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into both cultural-economic shifts in interwar Japan and the impact of deteriorating bilateral relations on international sports exchanges. The 1931 report illuminates the intersection of the Great Depression and Westernization, documenting how modern commercial entertainments like dance halls and cafés eroded the traditional geisha profession and forced women into hardship and pawning their kimonos. Home Ministry statistics embedded in the report provide quantitative evidence of the contraction of the geisha population in Tokyo and across Japan. Meanwhile, the 1940 cross-reference sheet demonstrates how rising geopolitical tensions between the United States and Japan increasingly intruded into non-governmental cultural spheres, complicating participation in international table tennis competitions.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.4062, covering indoor amusements, sports, recreation, and dancing in Japan) contains two records spanning May 1931 to February 1940. The first document is an extract from a periodic political report dated May 8, 1931, forwarded by U.S. Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes (originally filed under 894.00 P.R./41), concerning the severe economic distress experienced by the traditional Japanese geisha industry during the Great Depression. The report analyzes how the general economic downturn, compounded by growing competition from Western-style dance halls and cafés, led to declining patronage, pawning of kimonos, and a shrinking geisha workforce, as corroborated by official Home Ministry statistics. The second document is a cross-reference sheet dated February 14, 1940, referring to a State Department communication to the United States Table Tennis Association in Arlington, Massachusetts (filed under 032/1284), addressing whether diplomatic and political relations with Japan should influence American acceptance of an invitation from the Japan Table Tennis Association to participate in athletic competition.

subfiles.about: An extract from an embassy report detailing the severe economic decline of the Japanese geisha profession due to the Great Depression and Western cultural competition.
subfiles.summary: This document consists of a Document File sheet and an extract from Periodic Report No. 41 submitted by Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes on May 8, 1931, regarding the impact of hard times on the Japanese geisha industry. The report explains that the traditional geisha profession was severely hit by the economic depression and the rising popularity of Western-style cafés and dance halls, which drew away clientele unable to afford expensive geisha entertainment. Data released by the Home Ministry showed there were 80,717 geisha in Japan at the end of 1930, including 10,485 in Tokyo (a decline of 166 from 1929), with further decreases projected for 1931. Due to prolonged financial hardship, many geisha were forced to pawn their kimonos or abandon the profession entirely.
subfiles.title: Report extract on hard times in the geisha industry

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet concerning a Department of State letter regarding U.S.-Japan relations and participation in a table tennis competition.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes a State Department letter dated February 14, 1940, addressed to the United States Table Tennis Association in Arlington, Massachusetts, filed under decimal file 032/1284. The underlying correspondence comments on bilateral relations with Japan that might have a bearing on whether the American association should accept an invitation from the Japan Table Tennis Association to participate in athletic competition. The original paper is maintained in the State Department's general decimal records.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet regarding Japan Table Tennis Association invitation
